verify_session (identity.rs:1442) joins effective_platform_roles, but PROFILE (subject_export.rs:147) reads the role in a later snapshot, so a role revoked in that window yields null; a test cannot interleave the two statements.

details.description: Stored JSON incident payload, not a serde DTO. Fields vary by producer/kind; readers do not deserialize or close this map. Every *_microusd value is a non-null integer micro-USD string (unknown cost is reported in unknown_cost_requests, never as null). Each alerts.rs producer field is typed individually: pending_microusd is sum(held - held_unknown) read from budget_totals with no sign guard (migration 0015 has no >= 0 check), so drifted accounting can make it negative and it is signed; used_microusd (an incident needs used to reach a positive threshold of a positive reference), budget_microusd, spend_amount_microusd and min_spend_microusd (validated positive amounts), and current_microusd, baseline_total_microusd and baseline_hourly_microusd (settled ledger sums, CHECK(actual_microusd >= 0)) are unsigned. Any other *_microusd value from a producer not listed must still be an integer string (signed form). Admission-ceiling identity redaction is constrained by the separate variants below.

SettingsEmailInput.description: Closed serde struct object, or positional array [host, port, tls, username, password_ref, from_address, from_name] whose element types are deserialization-level only (the handler applies the same rules). Trimmed blanks mean absent; the host is lowercased; a username and its password reference come together. oneOf.description: A relay without credentials: host, port 1-65535, tls and a sender address; plaintext (`none`) only to a loopback host. from_address.description: A mailbox address as the handler trims and checks it: at most 320 BYTES (directory.rs email_valid), exactly one `@`, no whitespace or control character, and a lettre `Address` parse (the local part at most 64 characters). The pattern models only the character classes (no whitespace or control character anywhere, no ASCII punctuation in the domain); lettre's finer local-part and domain grammar (consecutive dots, labels over 63 characters, the 64-character local part, the 320-byte total) is not modelled, and the handler refuses what it forbids.

host.description: A DNS name or IP literal. Known divergences, pinned in the fixture tests: the handler (email.rs valid_host) refuses a host longer than 253 bytes and a string with a colon that is not an IP address (for example `1:2`), both of which this pattern accepts; and it strips any run of surrounding brackets before parsing an address (trim_matches), so with tls none it accepts the loopback spellings `[[::1]]`, `[::1` and `::1]`, which this pattern refuses (one balanced pair only).

port.description: An integer 1-65535. The handler deserializes an i32, so a float spelling such as 25.0 is refused (400), although a JSON Schema validator treats 25.0 as the integer 25.

tls.description: starttls, implicit or none; the handler trims surrounding whitespace (text()) before matching, so ` none ` is accepted. Responses always carry the bare value.

SettingsWorkspaceAlertEvent.description: Closed envelope shared by every alert incident variant: identity and lifecycle fields. Every incident has its `fired` email delivery (each producer inserts it in the incident's own transaction, deliveries are immutable), so `email` is never null. `cleared_email` exists only for a cleared incident (alerts.rs resolve: superseded and rule_disabled never enqueue one, and a silently cleared key-expiry reminder or aged-hold incident has none); a cleared incident of a rule kind (budget, spend, spike, error rate, provider, batch, admission ceiling; never a built-in, which includes the personal budget alert, never a key reminder or an aged hold) always has one: every `cleared` resolution of a rule incident goes through alerts.rs resolve, which inserts the `resolved` delivery in the same transaction. The variants (installation rules by kind, built-ins, aged holds, admission ceilings, workspace rules by kind, personal budget, key expiry) pin rule, workspace, connection, kind and the closed per-kind details exactly; this base `details` is the reviewed stored producer-specific JSON. This is the base of the workspace history: a workspace history always names its workspace and never carries a connection, so those two fields are fixed here, and only the rule slot varies (null for built-ins, key reminders and aged holds).

details.$comment: Workspace history rows return alert_events.details verbatim as stored producer-specific JSON; monetary refinements apply on this shared base, and every concrete workspace event variant refines it with the closed schema of its kind (Settings*Details).
details.description: Stored JSON incident payload, not a serde DTO; its fields depend on the kind. Every event variant binds it to the closed Settings*Details schema of that kind, so an identity can never be added silently. Monetary fields remain integer micro-USD strings.

info.description: INCOMPLETE contract skeleton (#81 PR1). Access extensions are minimum boundaries, not complete authority. Live owner, role, membership, personal-workspace and object-visibility checks remain authoritative. Personal details are owner-only; platform totals do not grant personal detail access. Shared members see their own activity unless an administrator or the object's visibility permits more; ownership checks can hide objects with 404. Auditor platform authority is read-only, independent User/membership entitlements remain usable. Credential families are exclusive, duplicate Authorization headers are refused, inference keys never authorize management, undeclared routes fail closed, and write scopes do not imply read scopes. BrowserAdminOnly includes Platform Admin even on GET. HEAD implicitly follows GET unless separately declared; no synthetic HEAD operations are listed. Request/response placeholders live in x-omg-request-schema and x-omg-response-schema until actual body presence, status and media types are reviewed; they are not permissive acceptance schemas. No universally enveloped error response is promised.
